questions.stem: On admission, the nurse scores a client's Braden Scale subscales as follows: sensory perception 2, moisture 2, activity 1, mobility 2, nutrition 2, and friction and shear 1. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: Total score 10: high risk for pressure injury; start a full prevention plan now
Total score 10: low risk for pressure injury; continue routine daily skin checks
Total score 14: moderate risk for pressure injury; reassess in one week
Total score 18: no risk for pressure injury; prevention measures are not needed
rationales: Correct. The six subscales add up to 10. On the Braden Scale, lower scores mean higher risk, and a score of 10 to 12 is high risk, so prevention (repositioning, support surface, moisture and nutrition care) starts right away.
The arithmetic is right but the interpretation is reversed: on the Braden Scale a low total score means high risk, not low risk.
The subscales add up to 10, not 14. Risk is also reassessed regularly (for example daily in acute care and with any change), not weekly.
The subscales add up to 10, not 18. Even a score of 18 or lower signals some risk, so prevention would still be needed.
questions.takeaway: On the Braden Scale (6-23), the lower the score, the higher the pressure injury risk; 18 or below means the client is at risk.

questions.stem: A bedbound client with urinary and fecal incontinence is at high risk for pressure injury. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Massage reddened skin over the sacrum to improve blood flow
Cleanse the skin promptly after each episode with a pH-balanced, no-rinse cleanser
Apply a moisture barrier cream or ointment to the perineal and sacral skin
Dry the skin by rubbing it briskly with a towel after cleansing
Use one breathable underpad instead of several layers of linen under the client
Keep the skin covered with a plastic-backed pad to protect the mattress
rationales: Massaging reddened areas over bony prominences can damage fragile tissue and is not recommended.
Correct. Prompt, gentle cleansing removes urine and stool, which break down the skin and raise the risk of pressure injury and incontinence-associated dermatitis.
Correct. A barrier product protects the skin from repeated exposure to moisture and irritants.
Brisk rubbing causes friction injury; the skin should be patted dry.
Correct. Extra layers of linen and pads trap moisture and reduce the effect of a pressure-redistribution surface.
Plastic-backed pads hold moisture and heat against the skin, which macerates it.
questions.takeaway: Manage moisture by cleansing gently after every incontinence episode, using a barrier product and keeping layers under the client to a minimum.

questions.stem: A client with a thoracic spinal cord injury uses a wheelchair and has full use of the arms. When should the nurse teach the client to perform pressure-relief weight shifts while sitting?
options: Every 2 hours, the same as turning in bed
Every 15 minutes while up in the chair
Only when the skin over the buttocks feels sore
Once each hour, unless the cushion is a gel cushion
rationales: A 2-hour interval is a starting point for turning in bed; sitting concentrates pressure, so weight shifts are needed much more often.

Correct. Seated clients put high pressure on a small area (the ischial tuberosities). Clients who can shift their own weight are taught to do so frequently, about every 15 minutes (lifting, leaning forward or leaning side to side).
This client has impaired sensation below the injury and may not feel discomfort until damage has occurred.
A pressure-redistribution cushion helps, but it does not replace frequent weight shifts, and hourly shifts are too infrequent for a client who can do them independently.
questions.takeaway: Clients who sit for long periods and can move themselves should shift their weight about every 15 minutes; sensation loss means pain cannot be the cue.

questions.stem: A client with a stage 3 sacral pressure injury has lost weight and eats about half of each meal. Which nursing action best supports wound healing?
options: Limit fluids in the evening to reduce incontinence episodes overnight
Encourage a low-calorie diet so that less body weight presses on the sacrum
Offer high-protein, high-calorie snacks and fluids between meals and request a dietitian consult
Give large doses of vitamin C as the main nutrition measure for wound healing
rationales: Restricting fluids leads to dehydration, which worsens skin turgor and tissue perfusion and slows healing.
Calorie restriction in an undernourished client slows healing; protein and energy needs are higher with a wound.
Correct. Healing tissue needs adequate protein, calories and fluids. Nutrient-dense snacks and supplements, plus a dietitian assessment, address the client's poor intake and weight loss.
Vitamin and mineral supplements are only advised when a deficiency is suspected; they do not replace adequate protein and calories.
questions.takeaway: Wound healing depends on enough protein, calories and fluids; involve the dietitian early when intake is poor or weight is dropping.

questions.stem: A client at very high risk for pressure injury is placed on a low-air-loss mattress. When the nurse enters the room, the assistive staff member has placed two folded bath blankets and a cloth incontinence pad under the client. What should the nurse do?
options: Leave the blankets in place because they add cushioning to the mattress
Add a sheepskin on top of the blankets to reduce friction
Turn off the air flow so the blankets lie flat and do not wrinkle
Remove the extra layers, leaving only the fitted sheet and a single breathable pad
rationales: Extra linen does not add useful cushioning; it blocks air flow, traps moisture and can create creases that increase pressure.
Adding more layers worsens the problem; the surface works best with minimal linen.
Turning off air flow removes the benefit of the surface and leaves the client on an unsupported mattress.
Correct. Each added layer reduces the pressure-redistribution and microclimate (air flow) effects of the surface. Only the minimum linen recommended for the surface should be used.
questions.takeaway: Keep linen and pads under the client to a minimum on a pressure-redistribution surface; layers defeat its pressure and moisture control.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses four areas of skin damage on clients who are at risk for pressure injury. For each finding, indicate the correct stage.
rows: Intact skin over the sacrum with a localized area of redness that does not blanch
Shallow open wound on the coccyx with a pink, moist wound bed and no slough
Full-thickness wound on the hip with the base completely covered by yellow slough
Intact, serum-filled blister over the heel
rationales: Nonblanchable redness of intact skin is a stage 1 pressure injury.
Partial-thickness loss with exposed pink, moist dermis and no slough is a stage 2 pressure injury.
When slough or eschar hides the wound base, the depth cannot be seen, so the injury is unstageable until the base is visible.
An intact or ruptured serum-filled blister is stage 2. (A blood-filled blister would suggest a deep tissue pressure injury.)
questions.takeaway: If slough or eschar hides the wound base, document 'unstageable'; serum-filled blisters are stage 2, blood-filled blisters suggest deep tissue injury.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses a full-thickness pressure injury on a client's ischium. Which finding indicates that this is a stage 4 rather than a stage 3 pressure injury?
options: Bone can be seen at the base of the wound
Subcutaneous fat is visible in the wound bed
There is undermining along one edge of the wound
A small area of slough covers part of the wound bed
rationales: Correct. Exposed or directly palpable fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage or bone defines a stage 4 pressure injury.
Visible fat is typical of a stage 3 injury; it does not reach the deeper structures that define stage 4.
Undermining and tunneling can occur in both stage 3 and stage 4 injuries, so they do not decide the stage.
Some slough may be present in stage 3 or 4; only slough that hides the whole base makes an injury unstageable.
questions.takeaway: Stage 4 = full-thickness loss with exposed fascia, muscle, tendon, cartilage or bone; visible fat alone is stage 3.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses the sacral skin of a client with darkly pigmented skin who has been on bed rest for 3 days. Which finding should the nurse recognize as a possible stage 1 pressure injury?
options: Skin that has the same color, temperature and texture as nearby areas
An area that feels warmer and firmer than the surrounding skin and is tender to touch
A dry, flaky patch that the client says itches
A small scar from a previous surgery
rationales: Skin that matches the surrounding area in color, temperature and texture is not showing signs of pressure damage.

Correct. Redness may be hard to see in darkly pigmented skin, so the nurse also compares temperature (warmth or coolness), firmness or bogginess, edema and pain with nearby skin. A localized change like this suggests stage 1 injury.
Dry, itchy skin is a moisture problem (xerosis), not a sign of pressure damage over a bony area.
An old, healed scar is not a new pressure-related finding, although scar tissue should be protected because it is weaker.
questions.takeaway: In darkly pigmented skin, find stage 1 injury by changes in temperature, firmness, edema and pain, not by redness alone.

questions.stem: A client's stage 4 sacral pressure injury is now much shallower and filled with healthy granulation tissue. A new nurse asks how to document the wound. Which documentation is correct?
options: Stage 2 pressure injury
Stage 3 pressure injury
Healing stage 4 pressure injury
Unstageable pressure injury
rationales: Calling a healing stage 4 wound a stage 2 is reverse staging; it misrepresents how deep the original tissue loss was.
Reverse staging from 4 to 3 is incorrect; the original stage stays with the wound as it heals.
Correct. Pressure injuries are not reverse staged. Granulation tissue does not replace the lost muscle and other tissue, so the wound is documented as a healing stage 4 injury.
Unstageable is used only when slough or eschar hides the wound base, which is not the case here.
questions.takeaway: Never reverse-stage a pressure injury; document it as a 'healing stage X' injury until it closes.

questions.stem: The nurse is evaluating several wounds that are healing by secondary intention. For each finding, indicate whether it shows healing as expected or requires follow-up.
rows: Beefy red, moist, granular tissue filling the wound base
Thin pink tissue advancing inward from the wound edges
Rolled, thickened wound edges that have not moved inward in 2 weeks
Pale, dry wound base with a new foul odor
rationales: Healthy granulation tissue in the proliferative phase is red, moist and bumpy because of new capillaries.
New epithelial tissue moving in from the edges shows the wound is closing.
Rolled edges (epibole) stop epithelial cells from migrating and point to a stalled wound that needs reassessment.
Pale, dry tissue suggests poor blood supply, and a new odor can mean infection; both need to be reported.
questions.takeaway: Healthy granulation is beefy red and moist; pale, dry tissue, new odor or rolled, stalled edges mean the wound needs follow-up.

questions.stem: On day 8 after an abdominal laparotomy, the nurse palpates along the client's incision. The edges are approximated, but no firm ridge can be felt beneath the incision. The client has diabetes and has been coughing frequently. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
options: A ridge does not normally form until after the sutures are removed, so this is expected
The lack of a ridge means a wound infection is present and antibiotics are needed
The finding shows that a keloid scar is forming under the incision
Healing may be delayed, so the client is at higher risk for dehiscence and the finding should be reported
rationales: The healing ridge is expected by about the end of the first postoperative week, often before sutures or staples are removed.
Absence of the ridge points to delayed healing, not necessarily infection; there are no signs such as drainage or spreading redness here.
A keloid is raised overgrowth of scar tissue that develops later; it is not shown by a missing healing ridge.

Correct. A healing ridge (firm tissue under the incision from new collagen) is normally felt about 5 to 9 days after surgery. Its absence, especially with diabetes and coughing, suggests delayed healing and dehiscence risk, so the nurse reports it and reinforces splinting.
questions.takeaway: A palpable healing ridge by about postoperative day 5-9 is expected; if it is absent, suspect delayed healing and dehiscence risk.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses a client on day 5 after colon surgery. Which findings suggest a surgical site infection? Select all that apply.
options: Wound edges are approximated and staples are intact
Cloudy yellow drainage is coming from the lower end of the incision
Mild itching along the incision line
Redness and warmth spreading more than 2 cm beyond the incision
Oral temperature of 38.6°C (101.5°F)
A firm ridge can be felt beneath the incision
rationales: Approximated edges with intact closure are expected findings.
Correct. Purulent (cloudy, yellow or green) drainage is a sign of infection.
Mild itching is common as a wound heals and is not a sign of infection.
Correct. Spreading erythema and warmth around an incision suggest infection.
Correct. A new fever several days after surgery, together with wound changes, suggests a surgical site infection.
A palpable healing ridge around this time is an expected sign of healing.
questions.takeaway: Surgical site infection usually appears 3-7 days after surgery as purulent drainage, spreading redness and warmth, increasing pain and fever.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the records of clients who had abdominal surgery. Which client factors increase the risk for wound dehiscence? Select all that apply.
options: Body mass index of 41
Age 34 years and does not smoke
Long-term prednisone therapy for rheumatoid arthritis
Serum albumin of 2.6 g/dL
Walked in the hallway on the evening of surgery
Surgery done through small laparoscopic incisions
rationales: Correct. Obesity increases tension on the incision and is linked with poor blood supply to adipose tissue, raising the risk of dehiscence.
Young age and not smoking are not risk factors; smoking would increase risk.
Correct. Corticosteroids suppress inflammation and collagen formation, which slows wound healing.
Correct. Low albumin reflects poor protein status, which impairs collagen formation and wound strength.
Early walking helps prevent complications and does not raise the risk of dehiscence.
Small laparoscopic incisions carry a much lower risk of dehiscence than a large open incision.
questions.takeaway: Obesity, malnutrition (low albumin), corticosteroids, diabetes, infection and straining or coughing all raise the risk of wound dehiscence.

questions.stem: A client has negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT) on a stage 4 sacral pressure injury. For each action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated.
rows: Stop the therapy, apply pressure and notify the provider if bright red blood quickly fills the tubing and canister
Leave the foam dressing in place after the pump has been turned off for 3 hours
Check the dressing seal for wrinkles or gaps when the device sounds an air-leak alarm
Turn the pump off at night so its noise does not disturb the client's sleep
Record the amount, color and consistency of drainage in the canister
rationales: Indicated: Active bleeding is a known, potentially serious NPWT complication; suction can keep drawing blood from the wound, so therapy is stopped, pressure applied and the provider notified at once.

Not indicated: A foam dressing left in place without suction for more than about 2 hours no longer supports healing and can hold bacteria and exudate; per manufacturer guidance and protocol the nurse removes it and applies a moist (saline gauze) dressing or restarts therapy with a new dressing, and notifies the provider.
Indicated: NPWT works only with an airtight seal; leaks usually come from wrinkles, gaps or loose edges, which the nurse finds and patches.
Not indicated: Therapy is meant to run continuously (about 22 or more hours a day); turning it off overnight removes the benefit and leaves a saturated dressing in the wound.
Indicated: Monitoring drainage tracks wound status and detects bleeding or infection (for example, a sudden increase, frank blood or purulent drainage).
questions.takeaway: NPWT must stay on with an airtight seal; if it is off for more than about 2 hours, replace the dressing per protocol, and stop therapy and notify the provider for active bleeding.

questions.stem: A client has a circumferential full-thickness burn of the right forearm. Eight hours after admission, the hand is cool, capillary refill is 5 seconds, the radial pulse can only be found with a Doppler, and the client reports numbness of the fingers. What is the nurse's priority?
options: Notify the provider promptly and anticipate an escharotomy
Reassess the hand in 4 hours, because edema is expected after burns
Wrap the forearm snugly with an elastic bandage to reduce swelling
Apply ice packs to the forearm to reduce inflammation
rationales: Correct. Inelastic eschar around a limb, plus edema, can act like a tourniquet. Signs of reduced circulation and nerve function need prompt reporting, because an escharotomy may be needed to restore blood flow.
Waiting 4 hours risks permanent muscle and nerve damage; these changes need action now.
Compression adds to the pressure already caused by the eschar and further reduces circulation.
Ice on burned tissue causes vasoconstriction and further tissue injury and can lead to hypothermia.
questions.takeaway: Circumferential full-thickness burns can cut off circulation; check distal pulses, capillary refill and sensation and report changes for possible escharotomy.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses burn wounds on several clients. For each finding, indicate the depth of the burn.
rows: Red, dry, painful skin that blanches with pressure and has no blisters
Moist, very painful wound with intact and broken blisters
Waxy white, dry, leathery area that the client cannot feel
Mottled red and white wound with slow capillary refill and decreased pain
rationales: Redness and pain without blisters, like a sunburn, is a superficial (first-degree) burn.
Blisters with a moist, painful base are typical of a superficial partial-thickness burn.
Full-thickness burns destroy the nerve endings and look white, brown or black and leathery; they are not painful in the burned area itself.
A mottled, less painful wound with slow refill is a deep partial-thickness burn; it may need grafting, but it is still partial thickness.
questions.takeaway: Burn depth: superficial = red and painful; partial thickness = blisters or mottled, painful; full thickness = leathery, white or charred and painless.

questions.stem: A client is rescued from a house fire in a closed room. The client has a headache, nausea and confusion. The SpO₂ is 98% on room air and there are no burns. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
options: Oxygenation is adequate, so oxygen therapy is not needed
The pulse oximetry reading may be falsely normal; give 100% oxygen and obtain a carboxyhemoglobin level
The confusion is most likely caused by anxiety after the fire
Normal SpO₂ rules out carbon monoxide poisoning
rationales: A normal SpO₂ does not prove oxygen delivery is adequate when carbon monoxide is bound to hemoglobin.

Correct. Standard pulse oximeters cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so SpO₂ can look normal in carbon monoxide poisoning. Headache, nausea and confusion after a closed-space fire call for 100% oxygen by non-rebreather mask and a carboxyhemoglobin level (co-oximetry).
Attributing confusion to anxiety could delay treatment of a life-threatening poisoning.
Pulse oximetry cannot detect carbon monoxide; a blood carboxyhemoglobin level is needed.
questions.takeaway: Suspect carbon monoxide poisoning after closed-space fires; SpO₂ can be falsely normal, so give 100% oxygen and check carboxyhemoglobin.

questions.stem: A client sustained major burns at 0800 and arrives at the burn center at 1000. The provider calculates the fluid resuscitation volume for the first 24 hours. By what time should the first half of the calculated volume be infused?
options: 0800 the next day
rationales: 1800 is 8 hours after arrival; the clock starts at the time of injury, which delays needed fluid by 2 hours.
2000 is 12 hours after injury; this would under-resuscitate the client during the period of greatest fluid loss.

Correct. Burn formulas plan half of the first 24-hour volume for the first 8 hours, timed from the moment of the burn, not from arrival. 0800 plus 8 hours is 1600, so the remaining fluid must be given faster to catch up. The formula only sets the starting rate; the rate is then titrated hourly to urine output.
0800 the next day marks the end of the full 24-hour period, not the first half.
questions.takeaway: Burn resuscitation timing starts at the time of injury: half of the 24-hour volume in the first 8 hours, titrated to urine output.

questions.stem: The nurse is monitoring a 70-kg client during the first 24 hours after burns to 35% of the total body surface area. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected or requires follow-up.
rows: Generalized edema, including areas that were not burned
Hematocrit of 54% six hours after the burn
Urine output of 15 mL/h for 2 hours in a row
New hoarseness and drooling 4 hours after burns to the face
rationales: In burns over about 20% TBSA, capillary leak causes edema throughout the body during the first day.
Plasma loss into the tissues concentrates the blood, so a high hematocrit is expected early.
Adult urine output goals are about 0.5 mL/kg/h (about 35 mL/h for 70 kg); 15 mL/h signals under-resuscitation and must be reported.
New hoarseness and drooling suggest swelling of the upper airway, which can close the airway; this needs immediate action.
questions.takeaway: In the first burn day, generalized edema and a high hematocrit are expected; low urine output or new airway signs need immediate follow-up.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with open burn wounds over 30% of the body. Which infection control measures should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Perform hand hygiene and wear a gown and gloves when providing wound care
Give systemic antibiotics on a schedule to prevent wound infection
Remove fresh flowers and potted plants from the room
Use a dedicated blood pressure cuff and stethoscope for this client
Allow visitors with cold symptoms to visit if they wear gloves
rationales: Correct. Burn wounds lose the skin barrier, so hand hygiene and barrier precautions during wound care prevent cross-contamination.
Routine prophylactic systemic antibiotics are not recommended in burns because they promote resistant organisms; antibiotics are given for documented infection.
Correct. Plants and flowers and the water in them can harbor organisms such as Pseudomonas.
Correct. Dedicated equipment reduces the spread of organisms between clients.
Visitors with respiratory infections should not visit a client with large open burns; gloves do not prevent spread by droplets.
questions.takeaway: Burn clients lose their skin barrier: use strict hand hygiene, barrier precautions, dedicated equipment, and keep plants, flowers and sick visitors away.

questions.stem: A client with burns to 40% of the body surface area is hemodynamically stable on the first day after injury. Which nutrition plan should the nurse anticipate?
options: Keep the client NPO until bowel sounds return in 3 to 5 days
Give clear liquids only for the first week
Rely on IV dextrose 5% in water to meet calorie needs
Start enteral tube feedings early, within the first day after the burn
rationales: Delaying nutrition for days worsens muscle breakdown and impairs healing; early enteral feeding is preferred.
Clear liquids cannot meet the high protein and calorie needs after a major burn.
Dextrose 5% gives very few calories and no protein; it cannot meet the client's needs.
Correct. Major burns cause a hypermetabolic state with very high calorie and protein needs. Early enteral feeding helps meet these needs, protects the gut lining and lowers infection risk.
questions.takeaway: Major burns are hypermetabolic: start enteral nutrition early with high calories and protein.

questions.stem: A client with healing partial-thickness burns of the anterior neck asks for two pillows under the head for comfort. What should the nurse do?
options: Explain why pillows are avoided and place a small towel roll under the shoulders to keep the neck slightly extended
Give the client two pillows, because comfort promotes rest and healing
Position the client with the chin flexed toward the chest to relieve tension on the wound
Keep the neck in the position the client finds most comfortable at all times
rationales: Correct. The position of comfort for burns is usually flexion, which leads to contractures. For anterior neck burns, pillows are avoided and the neck is kept in slight extension, for example with a towel roll under the shoulders.
Pillows flex the neck, which allows the healing skin to shorten and form a neck flexion contracture.
Flexing the chin to the chest promotes contracture of the anterior neck.
The position of comfort (flexion) is the position that causes contractures; burn positioning works against it.
questions.takeaway: Burn positioning works against the position of comfort: keep anterior neck burns in slight extension, with no pillows under the head.

questions.stem: A client with healing facial burns turns away when the nurse brings a mirror and says, "I don't want anyone to see me like this, not even my kids." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
options: "Don't worry, after your grafts heal you will look just like you did before."
"You're worried about how others will see you now. Can you tell me more about that?"
"Your children love you and won't care about your appearance."
"Let's talk about something else until you feel more ready."
rationales: This is false reassurance; facial burns often leave visible changes, and the promise may not be true.
Correct. Reflecting the client's feelings and asking an open question shows acceptance and invites the client to talk about the change in body image.
This dismisses the client's feelings and closes the conversation.
Changing the subject avoids the client's concern instead of supporting the client to work through it.
questions.takeaway: Support body-image changes after burns by acknowledging feelings and using open-ended questions, not false reassurance.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with partial- and full-thickness burns over 30% of the body and reports severe pain. Morphine is prescribed. Which route should the nurse use during the first days after the burn?
options: Intramuscular
Oral
Intravenous
Subcutaneous
rationales: Absorption from muscle is unpredictable after major burns; drug can pool and then be absorbed all at once when circulation improves, causing an overdose.
Clients with major burns often have reduced gut motility (paralytic ileus) and may be NPO, so oral absorption is unreliable.
Correct. During the emergent phase, fluid shifts and reduced tissue perfusion make absorption from muscle, fat and the gut unreliable. The IV route gives rapid, predictable pain relief.
Edema and poor perfusion of subcutaneous tissue make absorption unpredictable.
questions.takeaway: In the emergent phase of a major burn, give opioids IV; IM, subcutaneous and oral absorption are unreliable.

questions.stem: A client is brought to the emergency department with flame burns to the chest and arms. Some clothing is still smoldering. Place the nurse's actions in the order they should be performed.
options: Insert two large-bore IV catheters and begin fluids
Remove smoldering clothing and jewelry to stop the burning process
Estimate the total body surface area burned
Assess breathing and give high-flow oxygen
Assess the airway for patency and signs of inhalation injury
rationales: Circulation follows: IV access allows fluid resuscitation for burn shock.
Stopping the burning comes first, because tissue keeps burning while hot clothing and metal stay in contact with the skin.
TBSA is estimated after the ABCs are managed and is used to calculate ongoing fluid needs.
Breathing and oxygenation follow the airway; oxygen also treats possible carbon monoxide exposure.
Airway is the first part of the primary survey; burns to the face or inhalation injury can cause rapid airway swelling.
questions.takeaway: Burn emergency care: stop the burning, then airway, breathing, circulation, then estimate TBSA to guide fluids.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to change the dressings on a client's partial-thickness burns. Place the steps in order.
options: Moisten and remove the old dressings
Apply the prescribed topical antimicrobial and a new dressing
Give the prescribed analgesic and allow time for it to take effect
Cleanse the wounds and assess them for signs of healing or infection
Perform hand hygiene and put on personal protective equipment
rationales: Moistening old dressings that stick to the wound reduces pain and tissue damage during removal.
The topical agent and clean dressing are applied last to protect the cleansed wound.
Burn dressing changes are very painful; premedicating so the drug peaks during the procedure comes first.
The wound is cleansed and assessed once it is exposed, before new products are applied.
Hand hygiene and PPE come before touching the dressings to protect the open wounds.
questions.takeaway: Premedicate before burn wound care, then use aseptic technique: remove, cleanse and assess, then apply topical agent and dressing.

questions.stem: On day 3 after burns to 40% of the body, a client's urine output has risen to 150 mL/h, the blood pressure is 152/90 mm Hg, and the nurse hears new crackles in both lung bases. IV fluids are still running at the resuscitation rate. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
options: The client is developing acute kidney injury from the burn
Burn shock is worsening and the IV rate should be increased
These are expected findings that require no change in care
Fluid is moving back into the vascular space, and the client is at risk for fluid overload
rationales: High urine output does not suggest acute kidney injury, which typically lowers urine output.
Hypertension, high urine output and crackles point to too much circulating volume, not shock.
Crackles and hypertension need action; the IV rate must be reassessed to prevent pulmonary edema.

Correct. About 48 to 72 hours after a burn, capillary integrity returns and fluid shifts from the tissues back into the vessels, causing diuresis. Continuing high IV rates can cause fluid overload, so the nurse reports the findings and anticipates a lower rate. Potassium can also fall during this phase.
questions.takeaway: After about 48-72 hours, burn edema fluid returns to the circulation: expect diuresis and watch for fluid overload and hypokalemia.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with cellulitis of the left lower leg and is receiving IV antibiotics. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Outline the edge of the redness with a skin marker and note the date and time
Massage the leg to reduce swelling
Elevate the affected leg
Keep the leg dependent to increase blood flow to the area
Monitor the temperature and report red streaks or rapidly spreading redness
rationales: Correct. Marking the border gives an objective way to see whether the infection is spreading or responding to treatment.
Massaging inflamed tissue causes pain and can spread infection.
Correct. Elevation reduces edema and pain.
A dependent position increases swelling and pain.
Correct. Red streaking (lymphangitis), fever and rapid spread suggest worsening infection that needs prompt reporting.
questions.takeaway: For cellulitis, mark the border of redness, elevate the limb and watch for spread, streaking or fever that signals worsening infection.

questions.stem: A client is being discharged after treatment for cellulitis of the foot. The client has athlete's foot and dry, cracked heels. Which instructions should the nurse include to prevent another infection? Select all that apply.
options: Treat the athlete's foot as prescribed until it clears
Soak your feet in hot water each evening
Apply moisturizer to the heels to keep the skin from cracking
Stop the oral antibiotic once the redness is gone
Check your feet and legs every day for cuts, cracks or redness
Walk barefoot at home so your skin can breathe
rationales: Correct. Breaks in the skin from athlete's foot are a common entry point for bacteria that cause cellulitis.
Hot soaks can burn the skin and dry it out further, creating more cracks.
Correct. Moisturizing keeps the skin intact so bacteria cannot enter through cracks.
The full course of antibiotics is taken as prescribed; stopping early can lead to relapse.
Correct. Daily inspection finds small injuries early so they can be cleaned and treated.
Walking barefoot increases the risk of cuts and other skin injuries.
questions.takeaway: Prevent recurrent cellulitis by keeping skin intact: treat athlete's foot, moisturize cracks and inspect the skin daily.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old client has a painful band of grouped vesicles on one side of the trunk that appeared 2 days ago. Valacyclovir is prescribed. What should the nurse emphasize when teaching the client?
options: Start the medicine right away, because it works best when started within 72 hours of the rash
Wait until all the blisters have crusted before starting the medicine
Take the medicine only on days when the pain is severe
The medicine will kill the virus so it can never cause another outbreak
rationales: Correct. Antivirals such as valacyclovir shorten the outbreak and can reduce pain and complications when started early, ideally within 72 hours of rash onset, and are taken for the full course.
Waiting until crusting removes the benefit; the drug works by slowing viral replication early in the outbreak.
Antivirals are taken on a regular schedule for the full course, not as needed for pain.
Antivirals do not eliminate the latent virus, which stays in the nerve roots.
questions.takeaway: Start antivirals for herpes zoster as early as possible, ideally within 72 hours of rash onset, and finish the full course.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client with shingles on the right side of the chest is recovering at home. The client's daughter is 20 weeks pregnant and has never had chickenpox or the varicella vaccine. Which instruction by the nurse is correct?
options: "Your daughter could catch shingles from you, so she should get the shingles vaccine this week."
"Keep the rash covered and avoid contact with your daughter until all of the blisters have crusted over."
"After you have taken the antiviral medicine for 24 hours, you can no longer spread the virus."
"The virus spreads only through sexual contact, so ordinary family contact is safe."
rationales: A person without immunity who is exposed to fluid from zoster blisters develops chickenpox, not shingles. The recombinant zoster vaccine is not used to protect a nonimmune pregnant person, and the live varicella vaccine is not given during pregnancy.

Correct. Fluid from shingles blisters contains varicella-zoster virus. Until every lesion has crusted, the client covers the rash, washes hands often and avoids contact with people at high risk, such as pregnant people who are not immune, preterm infants and immunocompromised people. The daughter should tell her prenatal provider about any exposure.
Antivirals shorten the outbreak but do not make the open blisters noninfectious; the client is contagious until the lesions crust.
Varicella-zoster virus spreads through contact with blister fluid (and, for chickenpox, through the air), not mainly through sexual contact.
questions.takeaway: A person with shingles can give chickenpox to nonimmune contacts until the blisters crust: cover the rash and avoid pregnant, newborn and immunocompromised contacts.

questions.stem: A client with a normal immune system is admitted with localized herpes zoster on the chest. The lesions are covered with a dressing. Which staff member should the charge nurse avoid assigning to this client?
options: A nurse who had chickenpox as a child
A nurse who received 2 doses of varicella vaccine
A pregnant nurse who has never had chickenpox or the varicella vaccine
A nurse who had shingles 2 years ago
rationales: A history of chickenpox is evidence of immunity, so this nurse can safely provide care using standard precautions.
Two doses of varicella vaccine provide evidence of immunity.

Correct. Varicella-zoster virus from the lesions can cause chickenpox in a person who is not immune, and varicella in pregnancy can harm the pregnant person and the fetus. Staff without evidence of immunity should not care for this client when immune staff are available.
A past episode of shingles means the nurse has already been infected with the virus and is immune to primary varicella.
questions.takeaway: Localized zoster in an immunocompetent client needs standard precautions with lesions covered; assign only staff with evidence of varicella immunity.

questions.stem: A client from a long-term care facility is admitted to the hospital with scabies. Treatment was started today. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Place the client in an airborne infection isolation room
Wear a gown and gloves for direct contact with the client
Keep contact precautions in place until 24 hours after effective treatment is started
Wear an N95 respirator when entering the room
Use dedicated equipment such as a stethoscope and blood pressure cuff
rationales: Scabies spreads by direct skin contact and contact with items, not through the air.
Correct. Gowns and gloves prevent transfer of mites through skin-to-skin contact.
Correct. The CDC recommends contact precautions until 24 hours after effective therapy begins.
A respirator is used for airborne diseases such as tuberculosis, not for scabies.
Correct. Dedicated equipment prevents spread of mites to other clients.
questions.takeaway: Scabies and lice need contact precautions until 24 hours after effective treatment is started.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches an older adult who has diabetic peripheral neuropathy about preventing burns at home. Which statement by the client shows understanding?
options: "I'll set the heating pad on high so it works faster, but only for an hour."
"I can fall asleep with the heating pad on if I keep it on the low setting."
"I'll test the bath water with my toes before I get in."
"Because I can't feel heat well in my feet, I won't use a heating pad on them."
rationales: A high setting can burn insensitive skin within minutes.
Even low heat applied for hours, as during sleep, can cause burns, especially in older adults with thin skin and poor sensation.
The feet cannot sense temperature accurately; water should be tested with a thermometer or the elbow.
Correct. Reduced sensation means the client may not feel a burn until the skin is damaged, so heating pads and hot water bottles on the feet are avoided.
questions.takeaway: Clients with neuropathy cannot sense heat injury: avoid heating pads on numb areas and test water with a thermometer or the elbow.

questions.stem: A school nurse finds live head lice on a 7-year-old during class. The parent asks whether the child must stay home until all nits are gone. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "Your child can finish the school day and return after the first treatment; staying home until every nit is gone is not needed."
"Your child must stay home until there are no nits at all in the hair."
"Your child must stay home for 2 weeks after treatment."
"Your child needs to stay home until the whole family has been checked by a provider."
rationales: Correct. Head lice are not a health hazard and do not spread disease. Current pediatric guidance discourages 'no-nit' policies; the child can stay in school and return after starting treatment.
No-nit policies keep children out of school unnecessarily; nits left after treatment are often empty shells.
Missing school for 2 weeks is not needed and harms learning.
Household contacts should be checked, but the child does not need to stay home while this happens.
questions.takeaway: Head lice are a nuisance, not a disease risk: children can return to school after starting treatment, and no-nit policies are discouraged.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing health histories during a skin cancer screening event. Which factors increase a person's risk for melanoma? Select all that apply.
options: History of blistering sunburns as a child
Regular use of indoor tanning beds
Eating a high-protein diet
Having many moles, including some that are irregular
A parent who was diagnosed with melanoma
Taking a daily multivitamin
rationales: Correct. Intense, blistering sunburns, especially in childhood, increase the risk of melanoma.
Correct. Tanning beds give off UV radiation and increase the risk of melanoma and other skin cancers.
Diet protein content is not a known risk factor for melanoma.
Correct. A large number of moles, or atypical moles, increases melanoma risk.
Correct. A family history of melanoma raises a person's risk.
A daily multivitamin is not a risk factor for skin cancer.
questions.takeaway: Melanoma risk rises with UV exposure (sunburns, tanning beds), many or atypical moles, fair skin and a family history.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a group of adults about protecting their skin from the sun. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Use a broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of 30 or higher
A base tan from a tanning bed protects the skin from sunburn
Reapply sunscreen at least every 2 hours and after swimming or sweating
Sunscreen is not needed on cloudy days
Seek shade when UV rays are strongest, about 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Wear a wide-brimmed hat and UV-blocking sunglasses
rationales: Correct. Broad-spectrum products protect against both UVA and UVB rays; SPF 30 or higher is recommended.
A tan is a sign of skin damage and gives very little protection; tanning beds increase skin cancer risk.
Correct. Sunscreen wears off, so it must be reapplied regularly and after swimming or sweating.
UV rays pass through clouds, so sunscreen is still needed.
Correct. UV exposure is greatest in the middle of the day.
Correct. Hats and sunglasses protect the face, ears, scalp and eyes.
questions.takeaway: Sun safety: broad-spectrum SPF 30+, reapply every 2 hours, seek shade at midday, wear protective clothing, and avoid tanning beds.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches a client with a history of basal cell carcinoma how to examine the skin. Which statement by the client shows understanding?
options: "I only need to check the areas that get sun, like my face and arms."
"Once a month I'll check my whole body with mirrors, including my scalp, soles and between my toes."
"I'll check my skin once a year, just before my dermatology visit."
"I'll only worry about moles that are painful."
rationales: Skin cancers can develop in areas that get little sun, such as the soles and scalp, so the whole body is checked.
Correct. A regular (usually monthly) head-to-toe self-exam, using mirrors or a partner for hard-to-see areas, helps find new or changing lesions early.
Yearly checks are too infrequent for self-examination; changes could be missed for months.
Most skin cancers are painless at first; changes in size, shape, color or bleeding are the warning signs.
questions.takeaway: Teach a monthly head-to-toe skin self-exam, including the scalp, soles and between the toes, and report any new or changing lesion.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching the family caregiver of an 88-year-old client with thin, fragile skin how to prevent skin tears at home. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Apply a fragrance-free moisturizer to the arms and legs twice a day
Help the client stand by pulling gently on the forearms
Pad the edges of furniture and bed rails that the client may bump
Encourage long sleeves and long pants to protect the skin
Bathe the client daily in hot water with deodorant soap
Keep your own and the client's fingernails short and smooth
rationales: Correct. Moisturized skin is more flexible and less likely to tear.
Pulling on the arms causes shear and friction that tear fragile skin; support the client under the arms or use a gait belt instead.
Correct. Bumping into hard edges is a common cause of skin tears.
Correct. Clothing gives a protective layer over thin skin.
Hot water and deodorant soaps dry the skin and make it more fragile.
Correct. Sharp or long nails can catch and tear the skin.
questions.takeaway: Prevent skin tears in older adults by moisturizing, padding hard edges, covering the limbs and avoiding pulling or friction on the skin.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old client bumps an arm on a wheelchair and has a skin tear with the flap still attached. Place the nurse's actions in order.
options: Gently ease the skin flap back into place with a moistened cotton-tipped applicator
Draw an arrow on the dressing to show which way to remove it
Apply gentle pressure to control bleeding
Cover with a nonadherent dressing such as a silicone dressing
Cleanse the area with normal saline and pat the surrounding skin dry
rationales: Realigning the flap covers the wound and helps it heal; it is done gently to avoid stretching the flap.
The arrow tells others to remove the dressing in the direction that keeps the flap down, preventing it from being lifted off.
Bleeding is controlled first so the wound can be seen and cleansed.
A nonadherent dressing protects the flap without sticking; adhesive strips and tape can tear fragile skin.
Cleansing removes debris; the surrounding skin is patted, not rubbed, dry.
questions.takeaway: Skin tear care: control bleeding, cleanse gently, realign the flap, use a nonadherent dressing and mark the removal direction.

questions.stem: A client with severe plaque psoriasis is starting oral methotrexate. Which teaching points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Take the dose once a week on the same day each week
Take the dose every day at the same time
Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medicine
Use reliable contraception during treatment
Stop taking folic acid while on methotrexate
Keep appointments for regular blood tests of blood counts and liver function
rationales: Correct. For psoriasis, methotrexate is taken weekly. Taking it daily by mistake has caused fatal toxicity; ISMP lists oral methotrexate as a high-alert medication.
Daily dosing is a dangerous error that can cause bone marrow suppression and death.
Correct. Alcohol increases the risk of liver damage from methotrexate.
Correct. Methotrexate can cause birth defects and pregnancy loss.
Folic acid is often prescribed with methotrexate to reduce side effects; it should not be stopped without the provider's direction.
Correct. Methotrexate can suppress the bone marrow and damage the liver, so blood counts and liver tests are monitored.
questions.takeaway: Oral methotrexate for psoriasis is taken once WEEKLY; teach no alcohol, contraception and regular blood count and liver monitoring.

questions.stem: A client with moderate to severe psoriasis is scheduled to start adalimumab. Which result should the nurse confirm before the first dose?
options: Serum potassium level
Most recent hemoglobin A1C
Results of tuberculosis screening
Results of a skin biopsy
rationales: Potassium is not specifically affected by adalimumab and does not need to be checked before the first dose.
A1C is not required before starting a TNF inhibitor.

Correct. Tumor necrosis factor inhibitors such as adalimumab suppress the immune system and can reactivate latent tuberculosis. TB screening is done before treatment, and positive results are treated first.
A biopsy is not routinely required before biologic therapy when the diagnosis is already established.
questions.takeaway: Before starting a TNF inhibitor such as adalimumab, confirm TB screening and check for active infection.

questions.stem: A client with onychomycosis of the great toenail is prescribed oral terbinafine once daily for 12 weeks. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: "I'll call my provider if my urine turns dark or my skin or eyes look yellow."
"My nail won't look normal right away, because the healthy nail has to grow out over several months."
"I'll let my provider know if food starts to taste strange or I lose my sense of taste."
"I'll stop the tablets after about 2 weeks if the nail starts to look better."
rationales: This statement is correct. Terbinafine can rarely cause serious liver injury; dark urine, jaundice, persistent nausea or right upper abdominal pain are reported right away.
This statement is correct. The drug clears the fungus from new nail growth, so the nail looks normal only after the infected part grows out, which takes months.
This statement is correct. Taste and smell disturbances can occur with terbinafine and sometimes last a long time, so they are reported.

Correct. This statement needs correction. Toenail infections need the full 12-week course; stopping when the nail looks better leads to treatment failure and relapse, because the infection is still in the nail bed.
questions.takeaway: Oral terbinafine for toenail fungus is taken for the full 12 weeks; teach that improvement is slow and to report signs of liver injury or taste changes.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching the parent of a 4-year-old with atopic dermatitis (eczema) about daily skin care. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Give a short bath in lukewarm water
Use bubble bath to soften the skin
Pat the skin dry and apply a fragrance-free emollient within a few minutes after the bath
Dress the child in soft cotton clothing
Choose wool sweaters to keep the skin warm
Keep the child's fingernails short
rationales: Correct. Short, lukewarm baths hydrate the skin without stripping natural oils; hot water worsens dryness and itching.
Bubble baths and fragranced products irritate eczema-prone skin.
Correct. Applying emollient soon after bathing seals in moisture and helps repair the skin barrier.
Correct. Cotton is soft and breathable and less irritating than rough fabrics.
Wool is rough and commonly triggers itching and flares.
Correct. Short nails reduce skin damage and infection from scratching.
questions.takeaway: Eczema care centers on moisture: short lukewarm baths, emollient right after, soft cotton clothing and short nails to limit scratch damage.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old client with plaque psoriasis on the arms and scalp says, "People stare at my arms, so I quit going to the gym and I don't go out much anymore." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
options: "It sounds like other people's reactions have been hard on you. How has this affected your daily life?"
"Psoriasis isn't contagious, so you should just ignore people who stare."
"You could wear long sleeves so no one will notice."
"Lots of people have psoriasis, so it's really not a big deal."
rationales: Correct. The client's words suggest social withdrawal related to body image. Reflecting feelings and asking an open question helps the nurse assess how much the condition affects the client's life and mood.
This gives advice and dismisses the client's feelings, which closes off discussion.
Suggesting the client hide the skin offers a quick fix but does not explore the client's feelings or the social withdrawal.
Minimizing the problem ignores the real emotional and social impact of a visible skin condition.
questions.takeaway: Visible skin disease can cause stigma, withdrawal and depression; explore feelings with open-ended, nonjudgmental responses.

questions.stem: A client in the final days of life is receiving comfort care. The client grimaces and moans with each 2-hour turn, and the family asks whether turning can be done less often. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Continue turning every 2 hours, because pressure injury prevention is required for every client
Adjust the repositioning schedule to the client's comfort and goals of care, while using a pressure-redistribution surface
Stop all repositioning and skin care for the rest of the client's life
Explain that turning cannot be changed without a new hospital policy
rationales: A rigid schedule that causes distress conflicts with the goals of comfort care; prevention is individualized at the end of life.

Correct. At the end of life, comfort is the main goal. Repositioning can be individualized and spaced out based on the client's wishes and comfort, with premedication before turns and a support surface to reduce pressure.
Skin care and comfort positioning still matter; the plan is modified, not abandoned.
The nurse can collaborate with the team to individualize the plan of care; no new policy is needed.
questions.takeaway: At the end of life, individualize repositioning to the client's comfort and goals of care rather than following a fixed turning schedule.

questions.stem: A client has a stage 3 pressure injury with a large amount of drainage that soaks through the dressing twice a day. Which type of dressing should the nurse expect to use?
options: Transparent film dressing
Hydrogel dressing
Calcium alginate dressing covered by a secondary dressing
Hydrocolloid dressing changed weekly
rationales: Transparent films do not absorb drainage; they are used for superficial wounds or to protect skin.
Hydrogels add moisture and are used for dry wounds, not heavily draining ones.
Correct. Alginate dressings absorb large amounts of exudate and form a gel that keeps the wound moist without letting the surrounding skin macerate.
Hydrocolloids absorb only light to moderate drainage and would leak and macerate the skin with this much exudate.
questions.takeaway: Match the dressing to the drainage: alginate or foam for heavy exudate, hydrogel for dry wounds, film or hydrocolloid for light drainage.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews wound care prescriptions for four clients. Which prescription should the nurse clarify with the provider?
options: Hydrocolloid dressing for a shallow stage 2 pressure injury with light drainage
Foam dressing for a stage 3 pressure injury with moderate drainage
Transparent film dressing to protect intact skin over the elbows
Wet-to-dry gauze changed three times a day for a clean wound filled with red granulation tissue
rationales: Hydrocolloid dressings are appropriate for shallow wounds with light drainage.
Foam absorbs moderate drainage and keeps the wound moist, which suits this wound.
A transparent film can protect intact skin from friction.
Correct. Wet-to-dry dressings pull away tissue when removed, including healthy granulation tissue, and are painful. A moisture-retentive dressing is more appropriate for a clean, granulating wound.
questions.takeaway: Clean, granulating wounds need a moist, protected environment; wet-to-dry gauze removes healthy tissue and should be questioned.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client in long-term care has dry, itchy skin on the legs and arms. Which bathing plan should the nurse implement?
options: Bathe with warm water and a mild cleanser, then apply an emollient while the skin is still slightly damp
Give a full hot bath every day with antibacterial soap
Use an alcohol-based lotion after bathing to relieve itching
Rub the skin vigorously with a towel to remove dry flakes
rationales: Correct. Aging skin makes less oil. Warm (not hot) water, a mild cleanser and an emollient on damp skin help hold in moisture and reduce itching.
Daily hot baths and harsh soaps strip natural oils and worsen dryness.
Alcohol dries the skin and makes itching worse.
Vigorous rubbing causes friction and can tear fragile skin.
questions.takeaway: For older adults with dry skin: warm (not hot) water, mild cleanser, gentle patting and emollient on damp skin.

questions.stem: During a skin assessment, the nurse finds red, tender areas on the tops of both ears of a client who has worn a nasal cannula for 4 days. What should the nurse do?
options: Tighten the tubing under the chin so it does not move against the ears
Pad the tubing where it touches the ears and check the skin under the device regularly
Remove the cannula for 2 hours to let the skin recover
Apply lotion to the ears and leave the tubing as it is
rationales: Tightening the tubing increases pressure on the ears and makes the injury worse.

Correct. These are early medical device-related pressure injuries. Padding the contact points (for example with foam) and checking under devices often helps prevent further damage while oxygen therapy continues.
Stopping prescribed oxygen is unsafe; the pressure can be relieved without removing the therapy.
Lotion does not relieve pressure from the tubing, and moisture under a device can soften the skin.
questions.takeaway: Medical devices such as oxygen tubing cause pressure injuries; pad contact points and inspect under devices regularly.
